We have talked a few times about pre-IPO perpetual futures: Some offshore trading platforms, most notably Hyperliquid/Trade[XYZ], [1] list perpetual futures contracts on big private companies that are approaching their initial public offerings. These contracts are bets on the future price of the stock, and it is not at all obvious that the futures price would closely track the actual stock value: The perps do not represent any claim on the underlying stock, they are in theory off-limits to investors in the US, existing shareholders of the underlying companies are probably not allowed to sell the perps to hedge their exposure, big institutional investors who might want to buy shares in the IPO are probably not set up to buy the perps to anticipate their demand, etc. The perps are in a sense just a recreational prediction market on the price of the stock, not a derivative instrument tied to the price of the stock by arbitrage mechanisms. But a really important thing we have learned about finance in the last few years is that prediction markets are pretty accurate. That is: If you have a platform where people can make real-money bets on some outcome, their bets will tend to give a pretty accurate and well-calibrated estimate of the actual outcome. Kalshi event contracts are not tied to, like, election outcomes or football scores by arbitrage mechanisms, and in the abstract Kalshi could just be wrong about everything. But in fact Kalshi publishes research showing that its markets are good at predicting stuff. And on the Money Stuff podcast , Susquehanna International Group prediction market trader Jeremy Maletz made the same point, noting that prediction market odds are well calibrated even when the volumes are not enormous. The wisdom of the crowd largely works. And so in fact there is a track record of pre-IPO perpetual futures on Hyperliquid being quite accurate, that is, predicting the opening prices of IPOs. Is there anything you can do about it? At a high level, there are two somewhat reassuring answers: Your bank might be able to get the money back. “Stealing your money,” in this context, means basically moving some money from your bank’s electronic ledger representing your account to another bank’s electronic ledger representing the thief’s account. Your bank can call the thief’s bank and be like “that was theft, give us our money back,” and the thief’s bank probably will. Banks are quasi-law-enforcement agencies, and they will cooperate to reverse fraud or theft. On the other hand, the theft might be irreversible. The thief might have moved the money to another bank, and then withdrawn it in cash from the other bank, used the cash to buy art or casino chips, and rendered the money untraceable and removed from the electronic system allowing its recovery. In that case, you’re not necessarily out of luck. Your bank might be out of luck. Your bank is required to have good cybersecurity controls, prevent theft, etc., and if it messes this up it will probably have to reimburse you . This means, effectively, that the bank’s shareholders have to reimburse you. The bank has, like, $100 billion of money in its electronic ledgers, of which like $90 billion belongs to depositors like you and $10 billion belongs to its shareholders. (The $10 billion is the bank’s “capital,” and the law requires banks to have at least some minimum level of capital as a percentage of assets.) If the bank loses $100 of your money, it might have to subtract $100 from its shareholders’ money and add that back to yours. You are protected. These answers are in various ways imperfect. There are scenarios where the bank might not have to reimburse you. (The term of art is that banks need to reimburse you for “fraud,” but not for “scams.” ) And you could imagine really bad forms of hacking — where the hackers take all of the bank’s money, or where the bank loses its ledger of accounts entirely — where these solutions wouldn’t work. The fund owned some Lehman Brothers securities, and when Lehman filed for bankruptcy those securities lost value and Reserve concluded that its assets were worth only $0.97 per share. It had “broken the buck”; investors who had expected the fund to always be worth $1 per share were now disappointed. Investors demanded their money back, and Reserve had to close down, liquidate the fund, and give all of its investors back their money at a loss. Ultimately it paid them $0.991 per share. They lost 0.9% of their money. This was a huge scandal . It doesn’t seem that huge? But this was all quite rational. You see, if Reserve had cashed out all of its investors at $1 when they asked for their money back, the first investors to get cashed out would all get back $1 and have no losses, but eventually the money would run out, and the last investors left in the fund would get back $0 and have 100% losses. That’s what a bank run is. The last 0.9% of investors would have had 100% losses. The other 99.1% of investors would have been perfectly fine. In some abstract sense, if you were an investor in the fund, you had a 99.1% chance of being fine, so there was really no need to rush to get your money out. But because everyone knows the dynamics of bank runs , by backward induction, everyone had to demand their money back at once. So they did: “In just two days, redemption requests surpassed $40 billion ,” out of about $62.5 billion of asserts, and the fund had to shut down. The losses were not large . But tiny losses, combined with a very well-understood snowball effect, were fatal. Everyone could look several moves ahead, and what they saw, several moves ahead, was bad. Markets are efficient, so the bad thing immediately came true. Please take our quick reader survey . Bitcoin oopsie For a while last year, the US stock market would pay $2 for $1 of Bitcoin . It is hard to convey now how weird that time was. If you ran a tiny public company in mid-2025, the very best thing you could do was acquire $100 million of Bitcoin to add $200 million to your market capitalization. If you happened to have $100 million worth of Bitcoin in mid-2025, the very best thing you could do was to plop it into a tiny public company in exchange for $200 million worth of stock. These companies were called “digital asset treasury companies,” or DATs. Everyone kind of knew this couldn’t last ( it didn’t ), so there was a mad rush to get these trades done before the party ended. In September 2025, a company called Datavault AI Inc. got into this game. Sort of. Datavault was a small public company, “a leader in AI-driven data visualization, valuation and monetization.” In mid-September, it had about 116.7 million shares outstanding , trading at around $0.30 per share, for a market capitalization in the ballpark of $35 million. On Sept. 25, it announced that it was selling 278.9 million shares, at a price of $0.5378 per share, to Scilex Holding Co., another public company focused on “acquiring, developing and commercializing non-opioid pain management products for the treatment of acute and chronic pain and neurodegenerative and cardiometabolic disease.” [1] Scilex was paying the purchase price in Bitcoin, valued at $112,915.52 per Bitcoin , meaning that Datavault got about 1,309 Bitcoin for its stock. [2] The stock promptly shot up, hitting a high of $3.118 in October, for a market capitalization of about $973 million. Datavault did not, as far as I can tell, call itself a “Bitcoin treasury company” or DAT, and the announcement of the deal focused on its strategic goals, not the Bitcoin stuff. In writing a prospectus for a frontier artificial intelligence IPO, you have to make choices about what to promise in your good vision of AI, and what to threaten in your bad vision. SpaceX went public this year promising “the largest actionable total addressable market (‘TAM’) in human history,” $28.5 trillion, which is a lot, sure, but still a finite number of dollars. OpenAI has raised money to build artificial general intelligence with the considerably more abstract promise that “it may be difficult to know what role money will play in a post-AGI world.” So the two benchmarks are something like “we will make more money than any company has ever made before” and “we will make money obsolete.” Anthropic is, by these standards, relatively sedate. From its founders’ letter: We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history. As one of the companies at the very center of that moment, we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better. Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles. Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it through. “Buy our stock for miracles” is pretty modest as AI hype goes. But it wouldn’t be an AI prospectus without threats.
